proxy_language: Classical Sanskrit (with Sanskritized court register; Pali/Prakrit as secondary)
proxy_rationale: 'The Many-Armed Court' is a fictional later court in South Asia, evoking multi-armed deities (Vishnu, Durga, Avalokitesvara) and a Sanskritic court tradition (sabha, rajasabha, durbar). Classical Sanskrit was the prestige language of South Asian courts across the subcontinent and Southeast Asia in the later first millennium CE and after, so it is the most defensible proxy; the culture itself is not an attested polity, hence medium rather than high confidence.
phonology: Vowels: short a i u, long a: i: u:, vocalic r, e, o (long), ai, au. Consonants: stops in five places with voiceless/voiced and aspirated series (k kh g gh, c ch j jh, t. t.h d. d.h, t th d dh, p ph b bh), nasals n n. m (velar and palatal nasals mostly allophonic), semivowels y r l v, sibilants s s' s., h, anusvara m. and visarga h.
phonotactics: Syllables (C)(C)V(C); heavy syllables (long vowel or closed) matter for metre and, via stress, for the accent. Initial clusters are limited (st, sp, sk, pr, kr, tr, sv, ky, etc.); medial clusters are abundant, but word-internal stop-stop clusters are assimilated (voicing agrees, e.g. vak + dana -> vagdana). Words end in vowels, or in m, h, n, t, k, s in citation; final stops are rare and usually voiced or devoiced by sandhi. No initial ng or ny.
orthography: Scholarly IAST transliteration: a, a, i, i, u, u, r., e, ai, o, au, m., h., k kh g gh n, c ch j jh n, t. t.h d. d.h n., t th d dh n, p ph b bh m, y r l v, s', s., s, h. In plain ASCII game spelling: aa ii uu for long vowels, sh for s' and s., ri for vocalic r, m for anusvara, ch for c, chh for ch. Diacritics are optional if the audit is ASCII-only.
morphology: Highly inflected, fusional: noun stems take 8 cases x 3 numbers x 3 genders (nominative -ah./-am./-a, accusative -am, instrumental -ena/-ya, dative -aya, ablative -at, genitive -asya, locative -e, vocative stem). Verbs have roots with guna/vrddhi grades and thematic classes. Derivation uses primary (krt) suffixes (-tr agent: dhatr 'creator', -ana action noun, -ti, -ta participle) and secondary (taddhita) suffixes (-ya, -ika, -ina, -vant/-mant 'possessing', -tva/-ta abstract). Names of places often use -pura, -nagara, -grama; names of persons/gods in stem or nominative form.
compounding: Compounding is the main naming device. Tatpurusa (determinative, modifier or dependent first, head last): raja-sabha 'king's court'. Karmadharaya (adjective + noun): maha-sabha 'great court'. Bahuvrihi (possessive, 'having X'): bahu-bhuja 'many-armed' (lit. 'having many arms'), sahasra-bhuja 'thousand-armed'. Dvandva (coordinate): mitra-varuna. Dvigu (numeral first). Avyayibhava (adverbial). Head is final; the genitive 'X of Y' is normally rendered as a tatpurusa Y-X in the opposite order from English (surya-mandira 'sun-temple', 'temple of the sun'), though a free genitive Y-asya X is also possible. Agent names: noun + -kara/-karta/-dhara/-da ('maker/holder/giver'): kumbha-kara 'pot-maker'. Final vowel of first member is usually the bare stem or a linking -a-.
noun_phrase_order: Adjective before noun and agreeing in case/number/gender; genitive before head noun; numerals before noun; relative-correlative clauses; in compounds the head is last. Word order is otherwise free (basic SOV).

sources: Macdonell, A Sanskrit Grammar for Students (1927)
Cardona, Sanskrit: Its History and Structure (various)
notes: No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word unless the language is Goidelic (it is not). Many Sanskrit words are shared across Indic languages; court-name forms ending in -pura, -sabha, -mandira, -nagara are conventional. Use bare stems as names, not full case forms, for a naturalistic place/title feel. For a Prakrit/Pali flavor, reduce clusters (e.g. sabha stays, dharma -> dhamma, putra -> putta, hasta -> hattha).
